newsitem.title: IRAN: U.N. concerned over Afghan refugees in Iran.
newsitem.headline: U.N. concerned over Afghan refugees in Iran.

text.p: An Iranian crackdown on foreign workers could lead to more than a million Afghan refugees facing a stark choice of returning to war-torn Afghanistan or destitution in Iran, a United Nations official warned on Monday.

"It may lead refugees with no other viable choice than either to become very destitute or return to Afghanistan," Pierre Bertrand, chief of mission at the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Tehran told Reuters.
Iran's labour ministry ordered local employers earlier this month to fire foreign workers, most of whom are Afghans working without papers in low-paid construction and agricultural jobs.
The move was part of Iran's campaign to fight high unemployment, officially put at about 11 percent.
Many Afghan refugees have had residence permits withdrawn and told either to return home or live in refugee camps.
"We are sparing no efforts to clarify the situation with those with responsibility for refugee matters...We are concerned about this," Bertrand said.

Other U.N. officials said that families had already approached the UNHCR after the crackdown and that people from Kabul were still arriving in Iran, fleeing renewed fighting close to the Afghan capital.
The Tehran government estimates that there are 1.4 million Afghans in Iran, a legacy of the 1979 invasion of Afghanistan by the former Soviet Union and the country's civil war.
Up to 1.5 million Afghan refugees have voluntarily been repatriated since 1993 but the country's deteriorating civil war has slowed the return of people to almost a halt.
"It has virtually come to a standstill...Voluntary repatriation is the best rule but the present situation does not allow this," Bertrand said, referring to the civil war.

Tehran has stressed its role as the world's biggest host nation of refugees -- who also include Iraqi Kurds and Iraqi Marsh Arabs -- and pressed for more financial help from the international community.
"Whenever Iran does not receive international aid for refugees it starts to pressure us to return home," an Afghan worker told Reuters earlier this month.
Some $18 million was earmarked by the United Nations for refugees in Iran in 1996.

The U.N. body had expressed its official concern and was seeking clarification from the Iranian interior ministry, which has responsibility for refugee matters, on the labour ministry's new employment rules, Bertrand said.
Currently just 21,000 Afghan are in six special UNHCR camps with the vast remainder scattered throughout Iran.
